idiom_name: precedence-climbing loop over func-valued parselets (go/parser and go/token shape)
implementation_notes: Go has no inheritance, so the parselet hierarchy collapses into a table of function values plus a recursion that compares the next operator's precedence - exactly what the standard library does: go/parser's parseBinaryExpr(x, prec1) consumes while op.Precedence() >= prec1 and recurses with oprec+1 for left-associativity, and go/token exposes Token.Precedence(), LowestPrec, UnaryPrec and HighestPrec for that purpose. Closures carry parser state without an explicit context parameter, and go/scanner (or text/scanner) supplies tokens when the syntax is Go-like; the stdlib parser is a working reference to copy, including its maxNestLev depth guard and bailout panic. Hand-write the table when error messages, recovery and AST shape are yours to control; use a generator (goyacc, participle) when the grammar is broader than expressions.
pitfalls: Token.Precedence() returns LowestPrec (0) for every non-operator token, so the loop must run with minPrec >= 1 and must check the token kind before trusting the value; otherwise it reads past the end of the expression.

Recursion depth tracks input nesting, and go/parser itself guards with maxNestLev plus a bailout panic to turn stack exhaustion into a syntax error - copy that pattern instead of relying on the goroutine stack.

Mixing go/scanner token constants with a private precedence table is easy to get wrong, because token.Precedence only knows Go's operators; for a DSL define your own token type and precedence function and keep one source of truth.
